title.narrative: Number of laws blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

description.narrative: Laws blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

comment.narrative: Although Somalia Constitution provides for 30% quota for women in election position this is yet to be achieved. Somalia is still very much clan based and patriarchal society which excludes women from political and decision-making process. Article 27 on economic and social rights provide for affirmative action for women, the aged, the disabled and minorities. However, all these are yet to be achieved because of constant conflict and instability. Compared to Somalia, Somaliland is still lagging behind in terms of women's participation in leadership, political and decision-making processes. In Somaliland, there is only one female minister out of 28 and only two members of parliament out of 86. There is also a notable absence of women in the higher levels of government such as director general and head of department levels.
Advocate and lobby for the passing of the 2018 SOB or amendments to the bill that would protect women and girls against SGBV.

Although not completely achieved, legislative advocacy by WRA/Os on the SOB has greatly advanced women's rights. Accomplished by social media campaigns, media-oriented mass rallies, and discussions with parliamentary committees, Puntland's ratification of the zero-tolerance FGM bill stands apart. Still, difficulties exist since the Rape and Immoral Bill—formerly SOB—was first rejected because of misunderstandings and opposition. Notwithstanding political unrest and competing interests, ongoing advocacy by WROs/As, civil society organizations, and important ministries has helped the bill pass several review phases; it is now pending final review in parliament.
Advocate for the adoption of the 2018 SOB or amendment to better protect the rights of women and girls.
In 2021, the focus will be on mapping and identifying WRAs and Os to participate in the project, establishing coalitions, and engaging in capacity-building activities for the WRAs and Os. region.
Continue to lobby and advocate for the revision of certain chapters of the newly introduced Rape and Immorality Bill, which is still in Parliament.

title.narrative: Number of governmental policies & strategies blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

description.narrative: Governmental policies & strategies blocked, adopted or improved to promote women’s voice, agency, leadership, and representative participation in decision-making processes in public, private and civic sphere.

comment.narrative: Compared to Somalia, Somaliland is still lagging behind in terms of women's participation in leadership, political, and decision-making processes. In Somaliland, there is only one female minister out of 28 and only two members of parliament out of 86. There is also a notable absence of women at the higher levels of government, such as the director general and head of department levels.
Pushing for the 30% quota

Important government policies meant to increase women's involvement in decision-making have been adopted, thanks in part to the advocacy efforts of WROs and AS in Somalia. Their efforts produced a women's quota for the parliament of Somalia, adopted in April 2021. Still, just 24% of the federal parliamentary seats are occupied by women at present. This has led to demands for the quota to be fully applied. Notwithstanding opposition, ongoing campaigning by women's coalitions, CSOs, and political influencers effectively passed the one-man, one-vote election modality in parliament, which is expected to provide chances for political engagement for women and young people.

Advocacy and Lobbying campaign for Somalia women’s participation in the 2022 political process and to increase representation seats at all level of government bodies and leadership positions up to 30% (i.e. through National electoral law). We will also create strategic guidance frameworks to address the processes of inclusive politics and democratization in state-level elections and advocate for the role of women in the process through Civic engagement awareness, media campaigns and involvement in state-level electoral law process
In 2021, the focus will be on mapping and identifying WRAs and Os to participate in the project, establishing coalitions, and engaging in capacity-building activities for the WRAs and Os.
Still pending passage, the 30% women's quota is hence the target of continuous efforts.

Though not originally planned, the WROs/As in the Somalia region have been lobbying and actively advocating to increase women's job possibilities within the private sector, which is male-dominated. Private businesses were initially reluctant to hire girls and women. But thanks to regular communication and discussions with important private sector players, female staff members have grown rather noticeably in many different organizations. Though there is no evidence of any significant legislative change, the better job environment points to a good movement toward gender inclusiveness in the private sector.

title.narrative: Number of individuals (female) with improved attitudes and practices towards women’s voice, agency, leadership and representative participation in decision-making processes (youth)

description.narrative: Individuals (female) in the age between 18 to 35 years have improved attitudes and practises towards women's voice, agency, leadership and representative participation in decision-making processes (youth)

comment.narrative: In Somalia compared to other regions, the attitudes and practice towards women's voice, agency and leadership and representative participation in decision making processes is still very low. These are mostly dominated by male clan elders who control the political process. For example, out of the 20 women interviewed, only 7 reported having a positive attitude towards leadership and decision making, 1 reported to have ever participated in political campaigns; 1 reported to to have run for political office; 1 reported an interest in political affairs, 4 reported having knowledge on both electoral and governance process and only 1 perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants. In Somaliland, although still lagging behind, more women have positive attitude towards women’s voice, agency, leadership and representative participation in decision-making processes. In Somaliland, there are very few genuine spaces where women can come out and voice their concerns. Governance structures do not provide the necessary spaces to enable women to engage. The constitutional review process provides such space at the moment for women to engage. Entrenched clan-based culture, exclusion of women from political decision-making processes and asset ownership, high maternal mortality rates, rape, FGM, VAW, child marriage. Women’s access to justice restricted to formal, clan based and sharia-based judicial systems; Limited access to economic resources and assets; Low participation in politics and decision-making spheres.
30 Individuals (female) in the age between 18 to 35 years
This was not collected during the MTR and will be prioritized during the final evaluation

We will work towards reducing the barriers to women's participation in decision making processes by building their capacity on the available legal frameworks that supports them. NAGAAD and its partners will target individuals in the three specified regions; this will include women in their broader membership base, young women, local women civil society organisations, and women civic and parliamentary candidates to encompass both political, economic and cultural rights. Subsequently, the advocacy and lobbying arm of this project will heavily focus on influencers and policymakers at the national level. This includes the line ministries, media houses, Parliamentary Social Committee, members of Parliament in the House of Representatives and House of Elders (Guurti), political parties and their related officials, clan/religious leaders and the Electoral Commission. This diverse range of stakeholders are able to command various spheres of influence that NAGAAD hopes to tap into during the course of the five-year project. Overall 40 female youth targeted in Somalia and 15 female youth targeted in Somaliland.
Year one was mainly focused on mapping and identifying CSOs to establish coalitions, capacity strengthening of the CSOs or WROs/As to engage in advocacy and policy reforms

Summary of Baseline findings: Most of the activists are freelance and engage on issues supported by various organizations. Current leadership status among the participants varied across the countries; Regionally 55(50%), South Sudan 13(93%), Sudan 17(68%), Somaliland 4(57%), Uganda 16 (34%), Somali 2(20%) and Ethiopia 3(38%). Most of these leadership positions are held at the community level. Additionally, at WROs level, the average number of female staff across the countries is 167.5 while that of the male is staff is 23.3. Several women have risen to leadership positions across the surveyed countries. Somaliland had the highest number of women in leadership positions at 34%. This was followed by Ethiopia with 32%. The remaining countries, South Sudan, Sudan Uganda and Somali, had a mean of less than 10% The perception of participants in political affairs was also assessed. Although not very positive across the region except for Uganda, almost half of the participants 39(35%) perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants; Uganda 27(57.4%), Ethiopia 7(87.5%) while only Somali 1(10%), South Sudan 1(7.1%), and Sudan 1(4.0%) and Somaliland 2(8.6%). Structural conditions limiting women’s participation in decision-making roles include high levels of illiteracy; low levels of education, awareness of women’s rights, and self-esteem; lack of energy/time outside of economic activities; and high rates of VAW/G. Some women face more barriers than others: women from minority clans; internally displaced women and other migrants living in camps and informal urban settlements; poor rural pastoral women; women with disabilities; young women.

comment.narrative:
Somali women suffer unique challenges that undermine their potential for political participation and leadership. Influence on decision-making is strongly linked to family background and clan identity, with clan leaders and elders holding the ultimate decision power. Somali tradition inclines towards consensus-based politics, prevailing perceptions of women’s inability to reliably and legitimately ‘represent’ clan interests makes it difficult for women to feature in the clan negotiations. Minority clans low bargaining power within power sharing models translates to women from minority clans being doubly disadvantaged. Somali women are thus limited to influencing decision-making processes behind the scenes, often by advocating for a certain male representative, while opportunities to exert their constitutional right to political participation are slim to non-existent.
In Somaliland progress has been notably slower due to legal obstacles, the entrenched role of elders and more conservative ideologies. Successive proposals for women’s representation quota, including proposals debated prior to each of the elections from the first 2002 local council vote, through the 2003 (presidential), 2005 (parliamentary), 2010 (2nd presidential) and 2012 (2nd local council) votes, were unsuccessful37. As at 2020 there was only one female minister out of 28 and only two members of parliament out of 8638, women’s representation was limited to 9 local council representatives, one female member of parliament, and 2 female ministers (two full and one deputy). In Somaliland, women have less than half the opportunities afforded to men and are comparatively extremely disadvantaged across board, from fewer economic opportunities to, non-representation in political decision-making processes to lower educational attainments. Formal employment opportunities are limited, with women twice likely to be unemployed. Women’s access to employment is based on educational background, with higher education increasing the likelihood of labour market participation. In view of Somaliland’s largely informal economy, women with little or no formal education are particularly predisposed to vulnerable employment as self-employment or contributing family members. Moreover, women lack entrepreneurial skills, do not own property separate from their spouses and so lack access to financing to sustainably grow their businesses, and applicable terms and conditions to qualify for financing are often not suited for women’s small-scale businesses.

NAGAAD is currently working with 25 WROs who form part of the WCW coalition in the Somalia Region particularly from Mogadishu, Hargeisa, and Garowe and have been trained in advocacy and lobbying skills. In Puntland for example, 2 female members from the coalition were elected to the municipal council.
